items.title: 2026 Election by the Numbers
items.summary: A dive into the data shows just how historic the 2026 midterms were.

ai.sum: CFR published a data analysis showing how historic the 2026 US midterm elections were.

brief.summary: The author argues that the 2026 US midterms delivered a historic Democratic victory, with Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate and the party outperforming the 2026 polling averages by a wide margin. He situates the result against past midterms, noting that Democrats' House margin is the largest since 1990 and that their national popular vote lead ranks among the biggest midterm margins since 1942. The piece highlights record-level diversity and female representation in the next Congress, near-record turnout of about 49 percent, and Democratic gains in governorships and state legislatures. It also flags the shift in young and non-college voters, the failure of Republican mid-decade redistricting, and the possible activation of the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The author expects Trump to confront rather than accommodate the Democratic Congress, making the next two years likely to be turbulent.
brief.argument: The 2026 midterms were a historic Democratic rout that reset US political dynamics and set up a turbulent two years ahead of the 2028 presidential race.

items.title: Ukraine’s new drone blitz cuts Russian oil refining capacity by 30 percent
items.summary: Ukraine has renewed attacks on Putin's energy industry in recent days, conducting a series of powerful strikes that have reportedly cut Russian oil refining capacity by around 30 percent and sparked fuel shortages across the country, writes Peter Dickinson. The post Ukraine’s new drone blitz cuts Russian oil refining capacity by 30 percent appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Ukrainian drone strikes reportedly cut Russian oil refining capacity by about 30 percent, causing fuel shortages across Russia.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Ukraine's renewed long-range drone campaign against Russian refineries has been highly effective, hitting nine of Russia's thirty-five major refineries in ten days and cutting refining capacity by roughly 30 percent, according to Reuters. They describe the strikes as having paused in October under US pressure over fuel prices, then resumed after Russia kept bombing Ukraine's civilian grid. The piece says the campaign is seen in Kyiv both as leverage to force Putin to the negotiating table and as a deterrent against future invasion, given scepticism about Western security guarantees. It frames Russia's vast territory as a strategic liability against drone attacks and expects Russia to escalate airstrikes over the winter. The authors conclude that Ukraine's response will include further refinery strikes, though whether it can sustain the momentum is unclear.
brief.argument: Ukraine's renewed long-range drone strikes on Russian refineries are a strategic lever that is cutting Russia's fuel capacity and pressuring the Kremlin while serving as a deterrent against future aggression.

items.title: Europe sees surge in suspected Russian hybrid warfare incidents
items.summary: Europe has witnessed a surge in suspected Russian hybrid warfare incidents in recent weeks. This is fueling concerns that Vladimir Putin is escalating his intimidation campaign against Ukraine’s partners, writes Maksym Beznosiuk. The post Europe sees surge in suspected Russian hybrid warfare incidents appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Europe has seen a surge in suspected Russian hybrid warfare incidents in recent weeks, raising concern about intimidation of Ukraine's partners.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Europe is facing a rising wave of suspected Russian hybrid attacks that increasingly target ordinary civilians rather than only state institutions. They point to airport bomb threats across several European cities, media threats, and cyberattacks on supermarket freezer systems as examples. They stress that Moscow deliberately designs such operations to avoid attribution, using cyber capabilities, criminal intermediaries and disposable agents recruited online, which also compensates for expelled conventional intelligence officers. The authors read the trend as part of a Kremlin strategy to sap Western support for Ukraine while Russia struggles on the battlefield, and warn that gray zone pressure will likely intensify in coming months. They conclude that Europe should prepare for a prolonged campaign against civilian infrastructure.
brief.argument: Russia is escalating a hybrid campaign against European civilians to deter support for Ukraine, and attribution will remain hard by design.
recommendations: Prepare for a prolonged campaign of hybrid hostilities against civilian infrastructure
Protect critical civilian infrastructure of all kinds, including logistics and retail systems

items.title: How the Next Congress Can Repair the Military’s Personnel Crisis
items.summary: A change in Pentagon leadership won’t undo the purge of senior officers since early 2025, but the incoming Congress can begin repairing the damage by protecting promotions, guaranteeing women’s access to combat roles, and restoring oversight.

ai.sum: CFR published an analysis on repairing the US military's personnel crisis after a purge of senior officers.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a change of Pentagon leadership alone will not repair the damage done to the US military since early 2025. They describe a purge of senior officers, including disproportionate numbers of women and Black officers, and claim it erodes experience and the quality of decision-making. They point to polling showing many active-duty personnel fear politicisation and considering early separation. They contend that the next Congress should act through the FY2027 NDAA: tightening promotion processes so officers cannot be removed without cause or appeal, passing legislation to bar gender-based exclusion from combat roles, strengthening oversight, and reinstating the women's advisory committee. A next defence secretary should also recall experienced officers to duty. The piece treats these personnel measures as urgent priorities rather than optional steps.
brief.argument: Repairing the US military's personnel crisis, especially for women and senior officers, requires congressional legislation and oversight that outlast the current Pentagon leadership.
recommendations: Pass promotion-integrity provisions requiring written notice of cause and a right to appeal for officers removed from promotion lists
Enact the WARRIOR Act or similar language barring gender-based exclusion from combat units and fitness tests used to exclude qualified personnel
Strengthen congressional oversight of service chiefs and secretaries to reinforce apolitical norms
Reinstate the Defense Advisory Committee on Women in the Services and restore the historical record of women's contributions

brief.summary: The piece, a CFR roundup, uses reports of a suspected Chinese intelligence asset targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to examine four issues. The authors argue that export-control enforcement has gaps, notably chip sales to Southeast Asia and remote cloud access by Chinese firms, and that the Commerce Department is effectively outsourcing enforcement to companies. They say China is the most active foreign spy threat to U.S. firms and that defensive briefings are a key counter. They judge the allegations a new strain on U.S.-China ties ahead of a Trump-Xi meeting, where business ties to Beijing may shape policy. Finally, they note Nvidia's weight in equity markets and call for better oversight of systemically important AI firms, though investors so far see the risk as Nvidia-specific.
brief.argument: Chinese espionage against Nvidia exposes gaps in AI chip export enforcement and raises the stakes of U.S. AI governance and U.S.-China relations.
recommendations: Commerce should enforce existing licensing rules for untrusted firms in Southeast Asia and other countries ordering large numbers of AI chips.
Restrict Chinese companies from renting remote access to advanced AI chips they are barred from buying.
Cut off organizations known to work with Chinese intelligence from the most advanced chips.
Clarify which entity oversees systemically important AI firms and what guardrails they should face.

ai.sum: A Washington Times commentary argues the communist threat from China is being overlooked.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Western elites have consistently misread Chinese communism, treating the Chinese Communist Party as nationalist rather than a Marxist-Leninist revolutionary project. They trace this error to the Sino-Soviet split and to the engagement policy of the 1990s, which assumed economic liberalisation would weaken the party's political monopoly. Instead, they say Beijing absorbed Western capital, technology and markets while tightening political control, and that it is now positioned to export its governance model through economic dependency, military pressure and technological dominance. They cite the Cultural Revolution, Xi Jinping's ideological indoctrination and surveillance, and Western admiration of Chinese efficiency as evidence. Anti-Communism Week is presented as a call to restore the ideological clarity that sustained the Cold War effort, across both parties.
brief.argument: The West has misunderstood Chinese communism as nationalism, and its engagement policy has strengthened a Leninist party that now threatens the free world.
recommendations: Recover the ideological clarity of Cold War anti-communism in Western strategy toward China
Treat the CCP's Marxist-Leninist identity, not only great-power competition, as the basis of policy
Maintain bipartisan commitment to resisting communist expansion

items.summary: How Russian Sabotage and Social Media Fueled an American Panic bbert@hudson.org Tue, 11/10/2026 - 11:04 SVG Commentary Nov 9, 2026 Daily Wire How Russian Sabotage and Social Media Fueled an American Panic What was behind the recent prepper panic that had people emptying store shelves across the country? ai.sum: Hudson Institute commentary examines how Russian sabotage and social media fed a US prepper panic that emptied store shelves.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a wave of American public panic and emergency-supply hoarding was driven less by a real imminent threat than by the collision of genuine, documented vulnerabilities with sensationalist online commentary. They point to a false claim by Tucker Carlson that a US nuclear strike on Iran was days away, which they dismiss as fiction, noting that US Central Command has mostly maintained a defensive posture around the Strait of Hormuz and that breaking the nuclear taboo would be strategically indefensible. They contend that the real underlying concern is Russian hybrid warfare, including cyberattacks on food supply chains: refrigeration systems in European supermarkets and at six US military commissaries were disrupted. The authors note that government responses have focused on hardening industrial infrastructure rather than urging citizens to panic-prepare, and that existing 72-hour and FEMA guidance remains the appropriate baseline. They conclude that citizens should stay calm, prepare modestly, and be skeptical of viral online narratives.
brief.argument: Public panic over a looming catastrophe was driven by viral online fearmongering layered on real but mundane cyber vulnerabilities, not by an actual imminent nuclear or infrastructure threat.
recommendations: Harden industrial refrigeration and critical supply-chain systems against cyberattacks
Maintain the standard guidance of roughly 72 hours to several days of emergency supplies rather than panic-buying
Remain skeptical of viral online claims about imminent catastrophe
Sustain the Pentagon's FORTRESS initiative requiring bases to operate independently for at least 90 days

items.title: Materials matter: Managing critical commodities for the next-generation energy economy
items.summary: As economies electrify, demand will grow for materials such as copper, steel, and durable plastics that underpin the energy system. The post Materials matter: Managing critical commodities for the next-generation energy economy appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis examines supply risks for copper, steel and plastics as economies electrify.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the next-generation energy economy is a large physical buildout that depends on industrial materials, especially copper, steel, and durable plastics and composites, yet policy debate has focused mainly on critical minerals. They contend that each material faces distinct problems: copper supply is strained by rising electrification and digital demand against long lead times for new mines, steel remains emissions-intensive although grid and wind infrastructure need it, and durable plastics depend heavily on oil and gas. Their method is to examine how growth, energy system expansion and industrial change are reshaping demand, locate supply risks and market distortions, and assess policy responses. Their central message is that the energy transition cannot be delivered without these materials, so managing their supply chains will matter as much as deploying the technologies they enable.
brief.argument: Securing material supply chains for the next-generation energy economy requires industrial policies tailored to each material's production economics, supply vulnerabilities and innovation opportunities.
recommendations: Design industrial policy separately for each material, reflecting its production economics and supply chain vulnerabilities.
Extend policy attention beyond critical minerals to the broader industrial material base, including copper, steel and durable plastics.

items.title: “Endless Wars” Is a Catchy Phrase, Not a Reason to Shift Policy
items.summary: “Endless Wars” Is a Catchy Phrase, Not a Reason to Shift Policy bbert@hudson.org Tue, 11/10/2026 - 10:47 SVG Commentary Nov 10, 2026 Washington Post “Endless Wars” Is a Catchy Phrase, Not a Reason to Shift Policy What counts is not the length of the conflict, but the worthiness of the goals. Douglas J. Feith Senior Fellow Lewis Libby Douglas J. Feith & Lewis Libby Commentary Caption President Ronald Reagan addresses US troops on November 13, 1983, at Camp Liberty Bell, in…

ai.sum: A Washington Post commentary argues the term 'endless wars' should not by itself drive a policy shift.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the phrase "endless wars" is a rhetorical device that obscures the real question of whether a war's aims justify its costs, whether a workable approach exists, and whether continuing beats the alternatives. They support this with historical cases: Lincoln in the Civil War, Churchill in 1940, Eisenhower in Korea, and Reagan in the Cold War, all of whom persisted rather than retreat. They also show how a quick victory can be hollow, citing the 1991 Gulf War and Iraq under Clinton and Obama, where premature withdrawal produced renewed war. Fear of open-ended conflict, they contend, emboldens adversaries, who read democratic hesitation as weakness. The piece frames the current war with Iran as a long-running threat that justifies sustained effort, while acknowledging that reasonable people can disagree on necessity, objectives, conduct and endpoints.
brief.argument: Fear of "endless war" is not a sound basis for policy; the real tests are whether aims justify costs, whether a viable strategy exists, and whether continuing is better than the alternatives.
recommendations: Judge wars by whether their aims justify the costs and risks, not by how long they last.
Assess whether a workable strategy exists and whether continuing beats other options.
Recognise that a quick end can leave the underlying problem unresolved and produce further war.
Avoid rhetoric that signals reluctance to adversaries, since they adjust their strategies to it.

ai.sum: Hudson Institute authors argue that the transatlantic alliance needs a capital pillar.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the transatlantic alliance needs a third pillar beside military deterrence: control over capital. They contend Europe screens who owns its strategic assets but not who finances them, and that Chinese state-backed credit, buyer's credit, vendor finance and bundled construction contracts can create control that equity screening misses. They also argue that de-risking from China is an unfunded capital problem, since replacing vendors and restructuring supply chains require financing that banks, institutional investors, national public lenders and private capital each struggle to supply alone. Their proposed answer is a strategic capital facility with four eligibility tests (origin of funds, terms, embedded control, substitutability), a replacement window for excluded infrastructure, a European guarantee counterpart, and mobilisation of regional private investors, with US participation via the DFC.
brief.argument: Europe must extend its security screening to the origin and terms of financing and build a publicly backed, transatlantic capital facility so that rejecting risky Chinese finance is economically feasible.
recommendations: Extend EU investment screening to credit and quasi-credit exposures on critical infrastructure above a threshold, including vendor finance, leasing and bundled EPC packages.
Create a transatlantic strategic capital facility with EU and member-state first-loss protection, EIB/EBRD credit enhancement, and DFC participation, with private investors providing senior capital.
Establish a dedicated financing window for removing and replacing excluded high-risk vendor equipment in networks.
Consolidate or interoperate national export credit and political risk insurance agencies across member states.

ai.sum: The Atlantic Council argues Serbia's incoming government should keep the Vertical Gas Corridor project on track for energy security.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Serbia's new Student List government, which took office after the October 2026 election, should not let its September commitment to join the Vertical Gas Corridor lapse. They frame Serbia's energy system as fragile: lignite-heavy power, unreliable hydropower, and gas that is almost wholly imported from Russia via TurkStream at below-market prices. They contend the corridor, which would bring LNG from Greece and Azerbaijani gas north toward Moldova and Ukraine, adds roughly 1.5 bcm a year of import capacity by 2028 and would let Serbia meet its 2.7 bcm demand from non-Russian sources. The authors also argue the project fits the Student List's own platform on transparent contracting, a modern economy and private investment, and so lets the government pursue reform without forcing a choice between Brussels and Moscow. They stress that upcoming tests such as the first capacity auction and tendering will show whether the government follows through.
brief.argument: Belgrade's new government should keep the Vertical Gas Corridor commitment on track because it diversifies Serbia's gas supply and advances the Student List's own transparency, economic and investment goals without forcing a Brussels-or-Moscow choice.
recommendations: Keep the Vertical Gas Corridor commitment on track through the government transition
Use the corridor's first capacity auction and tendering to demonstrate transparent procurement

items.title: The six strategic mistakes that led to US defeat in Afghanistan
items.summary: Twenty-five years on, the United States' defeat in Afghanistan appears less inevitable than the result of decisions that undermined its ability to prevent the Taliban's resurgence. ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues the US defeat in Afghanistan resulted from six strategic mistakes rather than inevitability.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the US defeat in Afghanistan resulted from six discrete strategic choices rather than from the conflict being unwinnable. They say Washington tried to build a centralised Afghan state with a national army and Kabul supremacy, backing Hamid Karzai, which ran against the country's history as a loose confederation and fed Taliban propaganda about corruption. They add that the Bush administration's distraction with Iraq left the early Taliban resurgence unaddressed, and that Washington never pressed Pakistan hard enough over its sanctuaries and support for the Taliban and Haqqani network. The surge into Marjah and Helmand, rather than securing Kabul and Kandahar, squandered momentum, and firing McChrystal weakened it further. Finally, they argue the US missed a cheaper option in 2017: using money and contractors to rent the loyalty of regional power-brokers, as Najibullah had done.
brief.argument: The US lost in Afghanistan because of six avoidable strategic choices, chiefly the attempt to build a centralised state and the failure to pressure Pakistan, rather than because the war was unwinnable.
recommendations: Change as little as necessary: work with existing local power structures rather than imposing a centralised national model
Match force posture to the political goals set, rather than pursuing a light footprint alongside ambitious nation-building
Secure the population centres first and farm out outlying provinces to local allies at minimum cost
Use sustained, credible pressure on sanctuary states such as Pakistan, backed by willingness to act against them

Bessent clarified the intent as: “We…

ai.sum: Analysis proposes a US-China dialogue mechanism on AI and stability ahead of Xi Jinping's planned September 2026 White House visit, after Bessent met He Lifeng in New York.

brief.summary: The author argues that proposed US-China AI dialogues and communication channels are not arms control, since they lack enforcement or verification and leave AI innovation and power balance untouched. Instead they should be judged as confidence-building measures, drawing on Cold War precedents such as the hotline, Incidents at Sea Agreement and Nuclear Risk Reduction Centers. The piece sees real reasons for optimism, namely shared concern about AI's role in nuclear decisions, but notes that no AI-triggered crisis comparable to 1962 has occurred, that the two sides define key terms such as lethal autonomous weapons and human control differently, that AI is a general-purpose technology rather than a discrete weapon, and that private firms have interests that may diverge from governments'. The author says the first talks should focus narrowly on the 2024 agreement on human control over nuclear use, sharpen definitions, identify observable behavioural indicators, and avoid contentious issues such as export controls and AI governance. Domestic regulation of AI firms, such as incident reporting, is presented as supporting the credibility of bilateral measures.
brief.argument: US-China AI dialogues can reduce escalation risks only if they are scoped as confidence-building measures focused narrowly on nuclear-related AI risk, not as arms control.
recommendations: Keep the dialogue narrowly focused on human control over nuclear-use decisions and avoid broader disputes such as export controls and AI governance.
Use early rounds to sharpen shared definitions of autonomy and human control, including for early warning and nuclear command and control.
Identify observable behavioural indicators and escalation off-ramps rather than restricting AI development itself.
Build domestic regulatory mechanisms for AI firms, such as incident reporting, to lend credibility to bilateral measures.

They note Democrats won seats in traditionally Republican states such as Kansas, Texas and South Carolina, while some Senate races remain undecided. Trump downplayed the result and blamed fuel prices and weak candidates, while Vice President Vance placed primary blame on the Iran war. The piece contends that an opposition Congress will be able to chair committees, investigate, subpoena officials and delay nominees, including possible Supreme Court vacancies. It adds that impeachment is possible in the House but conviction would need a two-thirds Senate majority, a high bar.
brief.argument: The midterm results turn the election into a referendum on Trump's second term, and an opposition-controlled Congress will constrain his agenda even though removal from office remains unlikely.

ai.sum: Philippe Jaenada won the 2026 Prix Goncourt with a novel about a murder in Paris.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for Al Majalla, review Philippe Jaenada's Goncourt-winning novel The Unknown Woman of Quai de Javel, about an unsolved 1949 Paris murder. They argue the book's real interest lies less in the crime than in recovering the life of victim Louise Cansot, a Breton model in Montparnasse circles, and in the gap between documentary records and what imagination can reconstruct. The piece notes Jaenada's use of AI in research, which places the novel inside the year's authorship debate, and praises his reversal of the usual true-crime focus from killer to victim. It also flags a risk: the author's interventions and digressions sometimes crowd out the woman at the centre. Finally, it points to the concentration of all four shortlisted novels within one publishing group, Madrigall, as a structural issue for prize diversity.
brief.argument: Jaenada's novel matters most as an act of recovering a forgotten woman's life, using documentary inquiry while openly acknowledging the limits of knowledge and the writer's freedom to imagine.
